subject_entity.notes: Jewish-Christian sect insisting on full Torah observance and rejecting the divine pre-existence of Christ; active in Syria-Palestine and Transjordan; refuted by Irenaeus (AH 1.26), Origen, and Epiphanius; name means the poor.

object_entity.notes: Roman province encompassing the Nile valley; home of the Alexandrian church tradition and early monasticism.

evidence.notes: Irenaeus AH 1.26.2 describes Ebionites as present throughout the East including Egypt.

passage.excerpt: Those called Ebionites agree that the world was made by God; but their opinions with respect to the Lord are similar to those of Cerinthus and Carpocrates. They use the Gospel according to Matthew only, and repudiate the Apostle Paul, maintaining that he was an apostate from the law. As regards the prophetical writings, they endeavour to interpret them in a singular manner. They practise circumcision and observe the Mosaic law. They affirm Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary.

subject_entity.notes: Founder of Montanism (the 'New Prophecy') in Phrygia c. 155–180. Claimed to speak as the Paraclete in the first person. Associated with prophetesses Maximilla and Priscilla (Prisca). Montanism taught rigorous fasting, the imminent New Jerusalem descending at Pepuza, and the continuation of ecstatic prophecy — generating controversy with emerging episcopal authority.

object_entity.notes: Montanist prophetess and founding triad member alongside Montanus and Maximilla. Active in Phrygia c. 155–179. Her prophecies were recorded and cited by both supporters and anti-Montanist critics.

context_place.notes: Central Anatolian region in the Roman province of Asia; origin of the Montanist prophetic movement c. 170 under Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla.

evidence.notes: Eusebius HE 5.16 names Priscilla and Maximilla as Montanus's co-workers in prophecy.

passage.excerpt: There is said to be a certain village called Ardabau in that part of Mysia which borders on Phrygia. There first, they say, when Gratus was proconsul of Asia, a recent convert, Montanus by name, gave the adversary occasion, through his unquenchable desire for leadership.
passage.notes: Anonymous anti-Montanist source in Eusebius HE 5.16: origin of Montanus and his prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla in Phrygia.

subject_entity.notes: Second ecumenical council convened by Emperor Theodosius I at Constantinople, 381 CE. Affirmed Nicene theology against Arianism; expanded the Creed to include the full divinity of the Holy Spirit (against Macedonianism/Pneumatomachians); issued 15 anathemas against 'Origenism' (553 CE council also did this). Gregory of Nazianzus presided briefly; Gregory of Nyssa attended. Declared Constantinople second in honor after Rome.

evidence.notes: Socrates HE 5.8 explicitly dates the Council of Constantinople to 381 CE.

passage.excerpt: The council held at Constantinople in the consulate of Eucherius and Evagrius, which is the year 381, issued decrees confirming the faith of Nicaea and condemning the Arians and Pneumatomachians.
passage.notes: Socrates HE 5.8 dates and describes the First Council of Constantinople 381 CE.

source.notes: Online English translation (NPNF2 series).

subject_entity.notes: Hippolytus set himself up as rival bishop of Rome c. 217 after the election of Callistus I, whom he accused of modalism and moral laxity; sometimes called the first antipope; the schism persisted through the pontificates of Urban I and Pontian until reconciliation in Sardinian exile c. 235.

evidence.notes: Hippolytus Ref. 9.11-12 describes the schism with Callistus c. 217 CE; year inferred from context.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus alleged that the parable of the tares growing together with the wheat was spoken in reference to the Church: sinners should remain in the Church. He also affirmed that the ark of Noah was a figure of the Church, in which were dogs, hawks, and other unclean animals — so must the Church tolerate sinners.
passage.notes: Callistus defends leniency toward sinners using parables of tares and Noah's ark; penitential controversy
